title: Helping Others Achieve Mastery
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that the most talented team members have a strong internal drive toward mastery, and that leaders can motivate them by investing in their learning and skill development. It adds that getting better is a universal human need, so offering growth outlets to the whole team will be welcomed. The piece lists obvious investments such as formal training, after-action reviews, peer coaching and mentorship, alongside less obvious ones such as skill competitions and benchmarking trips. A notable move is to have high-drive members design and debrief their own learning programs, feeding ideas back into the team plan. It concludes that because mastery never ends, a leader's investment in it cannot be occasional.
points: The most talented team members have a powerful internal need for mastery, and investing in their skill development is a leader's secret weapon for motivating them.
Skill growth is a universal need, so learning outlets for the entire team are viewed positively.
Options range from training programs, after-action reviews and mentorship to skill competitions, benchmarking excursions and monthly skill assessments.
Asking driven members to design and debrief their own learning programs surfaces ideas to fold into the team program.
Occasional support misses the point; the learning investments must never stop.
quotes: Leaders who are attuned to which team members are unusually driven to improve possess a secret weapon for motivating them. They simply need to invest in their learning journey and skill development.

Although not everyone on the team is driven to improve and learn, getting better is a universal human need. So, providing the entire team with outlets for skill enhancement will be viewed positively by everyone.

In the obvious category, good leaders consider investments in formal training programs, after-action reviews following projects, online courses, peer coaching, job rotation, formal mentorship programs, and situation clinics, where peers discuss approaches to common problems.
Any experience that challenges the current skill level of team members can be highly motivational.
Asking them to design and debrief the team about their own personalized learning programs will often highlight new ideas and avenues that can be formally incorporated into the larger team program.
Leaders who only occasionally support a training program or provide the resources for a learning experience miss the point.
